1.title: Workloads and Controllers
1.text: Welcome to Module 3: Workloads and Controllers. This module is in the Kubernetes Fundamentals domain, the largest on the K C N A exam, and it covers the topic called Kubernetes Core Concepts. By the end you will be able to do four things. Explain what a Pod is and how its containers share resources. Describe init, sidecar and ephemeral containers, and the three probes. Compare Deployment, Stateful Set, Daemon Set, Job and Cron Job. And choose the right controller for a scenario.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Needs Its Shop Running
1.text: Here is Harbor Books. The platform engineer already has the container images from module one, and a cluster from module two. But the shop is not made of one kind of part. The storefront and the catalog can be replaced at will. The database must keep its identity. Every node needs a log collector, and a sales report has to run each night. Today each part is a plain Pod, and when one dies, nobody brings it back. In this module you pick the right controller for each part.

1.title: The Pod: the Smallest Deployable Unit
1.text: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share network and storage, and the containers are scheduled together on one node. They share one I P address and one port space, so they reach each other on local host. A Pod is ephemeral. Kubernetes never moves a Pod to another node. It replaces it with a new Pod. That is why you rarely create a Pod yourself: a controller creates and replaces Pods for you. Exam tip: Kubernetes schedules and manages Pods, not single containers.

1.title: Init, Sidecar and Ephemeral Containers
1.text: This slide is tagged moving, because one fact is tied to a version. Init containers run one at a time, in order, and each must finish before the app containers start. A sidecar container is an init container with the restart policy Always. It starts in the init sequence and keeps running beside the app. Ephemeral containers are different: you add one to a running Pod to debug it, and Kubernetes never restarts it. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, native sidecar containers are stable since version one point thirty-three. Exam tip: init containers finish and stop, sidecars keep running, and ephemeral containers only debug.

1.title: Pod Phases and Restart Policy
1.text: A Pod is always in one of five phases. Pending means the cluster accepted it, but its containers are not ready yet, perhaps because it waits to be scheduled or is pulling images. Running means it is bound to a node and at least one container is running, starting or restarting. Succeeded means every container ended successfully and will not restart. Failed means every container ended and at least one ended in failure. Unknown means the state could not be obtained, usually because the node cannot be reached. The restart policy is Always by default, or On Failure, or Never. Restarts back off: ten seconds, twenty, forty and so on, capped at three hundred seconds, which is five minutes. Crash Loop Back Off is a status you see in kube control, not a phase. Exam tip: there are five phases only.

1.title: Probes: Startup, Liveness and Readiness
1.text: Kubernetes has three probes. A startup probe asks whether the app has started. Until it succeeds, the other probes wait. A liveness probe asks whether the container is still healthy, and if it fails, the kube let restarts the container. A readiness probe asks whether the container can take traffic, and if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints. It is not restarted. A check can be an H T T P request, a T C P connection, a command, or g R P C. By default a probe runs every ten seconds and fails after three failures. The snippet shows a readiness probe on the storefront container, and a liveness probe that checks a T C P port. Exam tip: liveness restarts the container, and readiness only stops traffic.

1.title: ReplicaSet and Deployment: Who Owns Whom
1.text: A Replica Set keeps a set number of identical Pods running. It finds its Pods with a selector, it counts them against a replica count, and it creates new ones from a Pod template. It owns its Pods through owner references. A Deployment creates and manages Replica Sets. During a rollout there are two: the new one scales up while the old one scales down. The documentation recommends using a Deployment instead of a bare Replica Set. Exam tip: you normally create a Deployment. The Replica Set and the Pods follow from it.

1.title: The Deployment and the Rolling Update
1.text: A Deployment declares the desired state: how many Pods, with replicas, which Pods, with the selector, and what each Pod looks like, with the template. A rollout starts only when the Pod template changes, for example a new image. Changing replicas only scales. The default strategy is Rolling Update. Max surge and max unavailable are both twenty-five percent, so during an update at most one hundred twenty-five percent, and at least seventy-five percent, of the desired Pods exist. The other strategy is Recreate. Exam tip: change the Pod template to roll out, and change replicas to scale.

1.title: Rollout History and Rollback
1.text: These commands show a release. Set image changes the Pod template, which starts a rollout. Rollout status watches it. Rollout history lists the revisions. Rollout undo goes back to the previous revision, or, with to revision, to a chosen one. A Deployment keeps ten old Replica Sets by default, set by revision history limit, so it can roll back. A rollout that cannot make progress is reported after six hundred seconds by default, set by progress deadline seconds. Exam tip: rollout undo is the rollback command, and the old Replica Sets make it possible.

1.title: StatefulSet: Stable Identity and Storage
1.text: Use a Stateful Set when each Pod needs a stable name, stable storage and an ordered start. Pods are named with the set name and an ordinal, so db zero, db one and db two, and a Pod keeps its identity when it is replaced. A headless Service gives each Pod its own D N S name, and volume claim templates give each Pod its own volume. Pods start and update in order, Ordered Ready is the default, and the volumes are kept by default when Pods are deleted or scaled down. Exam tip: databases and clustered apps that must remember who they are belong in a Stateful Set.

1.title: DaemonSet: One Pod per Node
1.text: A Daemon Set keeps one copy of a Pod on every node, or on a chosen group of nodes. When a node joins the cluster, a Pod is added to it. When a node leaves, its Pod is garbage collected, and deleting the Daemon Set removes its Pods. Typical uses are a logs collection daemon, a node monitoring daemon and a cluster storage daemon. At Harbor Books it is the log collector on every node. Exam tip: one on every node means Daemon Set. It has no replica count.

1.title: Job and CronJob: Work That Ends
1.text: A Job runs Pods until a set number of them finish successfully, and it retries failures. The backoff limit defaults to six. A Job's Pods use the restart policy On Failure or Never. A Deployment allows only Always. A Cron Job creates Jobs on a schedule written in cron syntax, with five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week. The snippet runs the nightly sales report at two in the morning. The concurrency policy is Allow by default, or Forbid, or Replace. Exam tip: work that must finish is a Job, and work that repeats on a schedule is a Cron Job.

1.title: Choosing the Right Controller
1.text: Choosing the right controller starts with the nature of the work. Does the work end? If it runs once, use a Job. If it repeats on a schedule, use a Cron Job. Does it run on every node? Use a Daemon Set. Does each Pod need a stable name and its own volume? Use a Stateful Set. Otherwise, for Pods that can be replaced at will, use a Deployment. Exam tip: work out the nature of the workload first. The object follows.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Workloads
1.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Pod or container: the Pod is what is scheduled and managed. Liveness or readiness: liveness restarts, readiness stops traffic. Deployment or Stateful Set: replaceable Pods, or named, sticky Pods. Scale or roll out: replicas scales, and the Pod template rolls out. Daemon Set or replicas: a Daemon Set follows nodes, not a count. Job or Cron Job: once, or on a schedule. Exam tip: questions here usually describe a need. Name the need first, then the object.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. A Pod is one or more containers with shared network and storage, scheduled together and replaced, never moved. Init containers finish, sidecars keep running, liveness restarts and readiness stops traffic. A Deployment manages Replica Sets, a change to the Pod template rolls out, and rollout undo goes back. A Stateful Set gives stable names and volumes, and a Daemon Set gives one Pod per node. A Job runs work that ends, and a Cron Job runs it on a schedule. Now ten practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement describes a Pod? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes deploys: one or more containers that share an I P address and storage and are scheduled together. A group of nodes is a cluster, an image is the template a container starts from, and a Pod is not a virtual machine.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Harbor Books runs a Pod with an app container that serves the shop and a second container that ships its logs. How can the log shipper reach the app? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Containers in one Pod share an I P address and port space, so they can reach each other on local host. A Service is not needed inside a Pod, the Pod's volumes are not the only shared channel, and containers in a Pod do not get separate I P addresses.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A container's readiness probe fails, but its liveness probe still passes. What does Kubernetes do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A failed readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints, so it gets no traffic, while the container keeps running. Only a failed liveness or startup probe leads to a restart, and a probe failure does not change the Pod phase to Failed.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. The orders service needs about two minutes to start, and its liveness probe keeps killing it before it is ready. Which change fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A startup probe holds back the liveness and readiness probes until the app has started, so a slow start is not mistaken for a failure. Removing readiness, checking more often or stopping restarts does not give the app time to start.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. The storefront Deployment runs four replicas. The team changes the container image tag in its Pod template and applies the file. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Changing the Pod template triggers a rollout: the Deployment creates a new Replica Set and, under the default Rolling Update strategy, scales it up while scaling the old one down. Deleting all Pods first is the Recreate strategy, which is not the default, and no manual restart is needed.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A new release is faulty. Which command returns the Deployment named storefront to its previous revision? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Rollout undo returns to the previous revision, or to a chosen one with to revision. Scaling to zero stops the app, a restart re-creates Pods from the same faulty template, and pause only halts further rollout steps.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Harbor Books runs a database in which every replica needs its own persistent volume and a stable, predictable name. Which workload object fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A Stateful Set gives each Pod a stable name and its own volume through volume claim templates, with a headless Service for stable D N S names. A Deployment's replicas are interchangeable, a Daemon Set places one Pod per node, and a Job is for work that finishes.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Which statement about a Daemon Set is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A Daemon Set follows nodes, not a replica count: one copy per matching node, and a new copy when a node joins. A fixed number of Pods describes a Replica Set or Deployment, stable names and volumes describe a Stateful Set, and running to completion describes a Job.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Harbor Books must build its sales report every night at two in the morning, and the work ends when the report is built. Which object fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A Cron Job creates Jobs on a schedule, and each Job runs to completion. A Job alone runs once, and a Deployment or a Daemon Set keeps its Pods running instead of letting them finish.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Which pairing of workload and object is a poor match? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A database that needs stable names and its own volumes belongs in a Stateful Set, because a Deployment's Pods are interchangeable. The other three pairings are correct.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, C: a Pod is one or more containers sharing network and storage. Question two, A: containers in a Pod reach each other on local host. Question three, D: a failed readiness probe stops traffic, it does not restart. Question four, B: a startup probe holds back liveness during a slow start. Question five, B: a Pod template change creates a new Replica Set. Question six, D: rollout undo returns to the previous revision. Question seven, A: a Stateful Set gives stable names and its own volumes. Question eight, C: a Daemon Set runs one copy per matching node. Question nine, D: a Cron Job creates Jobs on a schedule. Question ten, C: a database needing stable identity is not a Deployment.
